title: Guided canvas build
summary: Build the classifier one component at a time, with concrete data, plain-language explanations and precise actions.
scope: Proposal only. Fifteen current v5 placement stages plus four library-overview fallback sections; no graph, placement order or saved-course identity change.
sourceChecks: The fresh guided canvas starts with Signal observations already placed; Place next adds the next component explicitly.
The supplied workflow-observations.csv contains 64 rows with signal, context and label. The current plan uses 25% Validation, 25% Test and seed 42.
Version5 has 15 actual placement stages. The rail uses ClassifierLessonGuide explanations and titles from WorkflowGuidedBuildPlan.
The model has two 2-to-8 branches, ReLU and Tanh, a 16-feature Concatenate and a final 16-to-2 Linear layer. Train owns mapping and run controls.

The four library-overview paragraphs are a separate fallback surface, not four extra placement stages. Native checks and any changes suggested by those checks wait for the completed Foundations chapter.
reviewNote: Review the 15 canvas stages first. The section picker also includes the four library-overview paragraphs, clearly separated. This packet proposes wording only; none of the Guided text has been applied. On integration, the older standalone reference view will reuse the four approved overview sections in place of its duplicated prose; its Start guided build action stays. Saved older guided-course versions keep their existing directions.

steps.title: Meet the classifier and its data
steps.text:
**What you will build**
You will build a model that puts each observation into group 0 or group 1. Classification like this can help sort messages or flag measurements for review. Here, the supplied file contains 64 made-up observations so you can learn the workflow without needing a real dataset.

Each row has three columns:
- signal and context are two measurements. These are the features: the information the model receives.
- label is the known group, 0 or 1. This is the target: the answer used to teach and check the model.

You will add a data path that chooses columns, reserves checking rows and scales measurements. A separate model path will turn the two measurements into two class scores. Train brings the prepared data and model together.

**Try it**
The source block, [Signal observations](kwip-node://data/observations), is already on the canvas. Select it and inspect its file in Configuration. As you follow this lesson, use Place next in Build this step to add each component with its supplied settings and connections. Reading Next does not place a component. Wait until the workflow is complete before running it.

steps.title: Choose the column types
steps.text:
**Understand the values**
A decimal measurement and a category number have different meanings. signal and context can contain decimal values. label contains whole numbers that identify groups; group 1 is not a larger measurement than group 0.

Casting means choosing how a column's values are stored. float64 stores decimal numbers; int64 stores whole numbers. This does not decide which columns become model inputs—that mapping comes later in Train.

**Try it**
1. Use Place next to add [Columns](kwip-node://data/cast), then select it.
2. In Configuration, inspect the column grid. Keep signal and context as float64 and label as int64.
3. Follow the table connection from Signal observations into Columns. After the complete workflow runs, you can inspect its output table to check the resulting types.

steps.title: Keep rows aside for checking
steps.text:
**Separate learning from checking**
Training rows teach the model. Validation rows show how it handles examples it did not learn from, helping you compare changes. Test rows are reserved for a final check after those choices are made.

Partition keeps 25% for Validation and 25% for Test, leaving half for Training. For the supplied 64-row file, that is 16, 16 and 32 rows respectively. A seed is a number that repeats the random split when the data and settings stay the same.

**Try it**
1. Place and select [Partition](kwip-node://data/split).
2. Keep the supplied random strategy, Validation 25%, Test 25% and seed 42.
3. Find its three table outputs. Follow them as you add the next component. Do not use Test results to choose the model's settings.

steps.title: Scale measurements using Training only
steps.text:
**Learn one shared scale**
signal and context use different ranges. Standard scaling puts each measurement on a more comparable scale: it subtracts the training average, then divides by the spread learned from those same rows.

Preprocess learns these rules from Training only. It reuses them for Validation and Test. Learning the rules from checking rows would let information from those rows influence training.

**Try it**
1. Place and select [Preprocess](kwip-node://data/fit).
2. Check that signal and context use Standard scaling. Keep label out of the scaling rules.
3. Follow its Training, Validation and Test inputs back to the matching Partition outputs. These roles must stay separate.

steps.title: Inspect the prepared Training table
steps.text:
**What has changed?**
Preprocess changes the two feature values using the training scaling rules. Each row still represents the same observation, and label still gives its known group.

View lets you inspect the table without passing data on to another tool. Train will receive its own direct connection from Preprocess later.

**Try it**
1. Place [Inspect prepared training observations](kwip-node://data/training), the first View block.
2. Follow its input to Preprocess's Training output.
3. Once the complete flow has run, select this View and inspect its table in Results. Compare the measurements with the original source. Do not expect captured output before the run.

steps.title: Inspect the prepared Validation table
steps.text:
**Use the same measuring system**
Validation measurements must use the scaling rules learned from Training. Otherwise, the model would be checked on numbers prepared in a different way from the numbers it learned from.

These are different observations from Training, prepared with the same rules—not a second set of scaling rules learned from Validation.

**Try it**
1. Place [Inspect prepared validation observations](kwip-node://data/validation), the second View block.
2. Follow its input to Preprocess's Validation output.
3. After the complete run, inspect its table in Results. The label values should still identify groups 0 and 1. Keep the Validation rows out of the scaling fit.

steps.title: Mark where measurements enter the model
steps.text:
**Read the model input**
[Measurements](kwip-node://model/input) is the Model input block. It marks where the prepared numbers enter the model. It does not read the CSV file.

Each observation supplies two numbers in order: signal, then context. Its sample shape is [2]. If four observations are processed together, the tensor shape is [4, 2]: four observations and two measurements per observation. Processing observations together is called a batch. A batch of one has shape [1, 2].

**Try it**
1. Place and select Measurements.
2. Keep Floating values and Features 2 in Configuration.
3. As you add the next layers, follow its outgoing tensor connections into both branches. Changing the batch size must not change the two features each observation supplies.

steps.title: Learn eight combinations of the inputs
steps.text:
**What a Linear layer learns**
A Linear layer combines the input values using weights and a bias. Weights control each input's contribution; a bias is an added offset. For inputs 2 and 3, weights 1 and 2, and bias 1, one output would be 2 × 1 + 3 × 2 + 1 = 9. Training adjusts the weights and bias.

This layer produces eight combinations of the same two measurements. Those eight values are learned features, not eight new observations.

**Try it**
1. Place and select [Branch A](kwip-node://model/branch-a), the first Linear layer.
2. Keep 2 input features and 8 output features.
3. Trace its input back to Measurements. A batch shaped [4, 2] becomes [4, 8]: the number of observations stays four.

steps.title: Change how the first branch responds
steps.text:
**Introduce an activation**
ReLU keeps positive values and changes negative values to zero. For example, [-3, 0, 2] becomes [0, 0, 2]. An activation changes how a model responds to values, allowing it to learn patterns that a chain of weighted sums alone cannot represent.

ReLU changes values, not the number of observations or features.

**Try it**
1. Place [Activation A](kwip-node://model/activation-a), the ReLU activation.
2. Follow its input from Branch A. It still produces eight features per observation.
3. After the full run, inspect its captured tensor if available. Look for zero or positive values; ReLU should not leave a negative value in this branch's output.

steps.title: Give the second branch its own weights
steps.text:
**Same measurements, separate learning**
The second branch receives the same signal and context measurements as Branch A. It has its own weights and bias, so it can learn different combinations.

Sharing an input does not mean sharing learned weights. Both branches produce eight features, but their values need not match.

**Try it**
1. Place and select [Branch B](kwip-node://model/branch-b), the second Linear layer.
2. Keep 2 input features and 8 output features.
3. Trace its input back to Measurements. After a run, compare the captured outputs of Branch A and Branch B without assuming they should be equal.

steps.title: Keep a smooth, signed response
steps.text:
**Compare Tanh with ReLU**
Tanh smoothly brings values between -1 and 1. Zero stays zero; large positive values approach 1, and large negative values approach -1.

Unlike ReLU, Tanh can keep negative responses. This gives the second branch a different response while preserving its eight features. Keeping values in a range does not, by itself, guarantee a better model.

**Try it**
1. Place [Activation B](kwip-node://model/activation-b), the Tanh activation.
2. Follow its input from Branch B.
3. After running, inspect its captured output if available. Compare its range with Activation A's output. Both still have eight features for each observation.

steps.title: Keep the features from both branches
steps.text:
**Join features side by side**
Concatenate joins the two branches without adding their values together. Each contributes eight features, giving 16 features per observation. Four observations therefore go from two [4, 8] tensors to one [4, 16] tensor.

Add would sum corresponding values and keep eight features. That is a different operation.

**Try it**
1. Place and select [Combine](kwip-node://model/merge), the Concatenate block.
2. In Configuration, check that both branches appear in Connected inputs.
3. Keep Join axis -1, meaning the last direction of the tensor: features in this example. Planned shape describes the expected arrangement; captured Output is available after a run.

steps.title: Produce one score for each group
steps.text:
**Turn learned features into scores**
The final Linear layer turns 16 learned features into two scores for each observation: one for group 0 and one for group 1. These raw scores are often called logits.

A higher score is the model's preference. Raw scores are not probabilities: they do not have to sit between 0 and 1 or add up to 1.

**Try it**
1. Place and select [Classifier](kwip-node://model/classifier), the final Linear layer.
2. Keep 16 input features and 2 output features.
3. Follow its output toward the model boundary. For four observations, the expected shape is [4, 2]: four observations with two class scores each.

steps.title: Connect the model to Train
steps.text:
**Define the complete model**
[Prediction](kwip-node://model/output) is the Model definition block. It receives the two final scores and exposes the connected architecture for Train to use. Its model connection describes the model; it does not carry rows from the source table.

The selected training rule compares raw class scores with the known labels. It handles the probability calculation it needs, so adding Softmax before this boundary would change the intended input to that rule.

**Try it**
1. Place and select Prediction. Follow its tensor input back to Classifier.
2. Inspect Model inputs in Configuration. Keep two floating-point features and the existing entry connections to both branches.
3. Leave the final two scores unchanged. The Model definition output will connect to Train in the next placement.

steps.title: Map the columns, run and inspect
steps.text:
**Bring model and data together**
Train uses the model, the prepared Training table and the prepared Validation table. Data mapping says which columns provide the inputs and which provide the answers. Keep signal then context as input features and label as the target. Including label as an input would give the model the answer instead of teaching it to predict.

An epoch is one pass through Training rows. A batch is a group used for one training update. The learning rate controls the size of changes to the weights. Loss measures prediction error under the chosen rule; accuracy is the fraction of correct group choices. Validation checks observations kept out of training.

**Try it**
1. Place and select [Fit and evaluate classifier](kwip-node://control/train), the Train block. Check its Model, Training and Validation connections.
2. In Configuration → Data mapping, check the ordered inputs signal, context and target label.
3. Review Run settings and Batches: begin with the supplied 3 epochs, batch size 32 and seed 42. Keep learning rate 0.03 in the optimizer settings. Partition's seed controls a separate random choice.
4. Choose Run this workflow or Run Flow. Clear the canvas selection to inspect global Activity and Diagnostics. Select either View block for its table, or Train's prediction-table output for the recorded predictions. Use History for saved versions and recorded runs; the available run details depend on capture settings.

Compare what you expected with the actual shapes, scores and validation result. A successful run does not prove accuracy on new data or award assessment completion. Save keeps your attempt; Start fresh opens a separate supplied canvas without discarding it.

steps.title: Meet the guided workflow
steps.text:
Build a small classifier that predicts group 0 or 1 from two measurements, signal and context. The supplied file contains 64 made-up observations. The data path chooses types, reserves checking rows and scales the measurements. The model turns two features into two class scores, and Train uses the known label to adjust its weights.

Open the guided canvas to place each stage explicitly. Reading a step does not change the canvas.

steps.title: Follow tables and tensors
steps.text:
Select a placed component to inspect Configuration. A table connection carries named columns and rows through preparation. A tensor connection carries arrays of numbers through the model. For example, shape [4, 2] means four observations with two values each; [4, 8] still has four observations, with eight learned features.

Follow the two model branches from Measurements into Branch A and Branch B, then into Combine. Use the guided canvas stages for the actual placement directions.

steps.title: Try one deliberate mismatch
steps.text:
After the guided placement is complete, select Branch A and change its input width from 2 to 3. Apply the change and inspect the diagnostic: Measurements still supplies two features, so this layer now expects a different width.

Restore 2 and Apply, or use Undo. Confirm the diagnostic clears before running. Changing an expected width does not add a third measurement to the data.

steps.title: Run and compare the results
steps.text:
When all components are placed, select Train. Check Data mapping: signal then context are inputs, and label is the target. Review the supplied run budget, then choose Run Flow.

Inspect captured tables at the two View blocks and the prediction table from Train. Clear selection for global Activity and Diagnostics. A completed run confirms that the workflow executed; it does not award mastery or guarantee predictions on new data.
